mainTopic: When a Jew is put in נידוי for hurting a fellow Jew through a gentile court or a gentile buyer: limits on the rule about a single witness, רב אשי's unresolved question about an אדם חשוב, and selling land to a גוי next to a Jew's field.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a rule from the previous amud: a Jew who testifies alone against a fellow Jew in a gentile court is put in נידוי. The rule is limited to a single witness, and only in a village court; the official court only imposes an oath on one witness, as the תורה does. רב אשי's question about an אדם חשוב, whom the gentiles trust like two witnesses, ends in תיקו. רב אשי then rules that a Jew who sells land to a גוי next to a fellow Jew's field is put in נידוי. The reason is not דינא דבר מצרא. It is that he 'placed a lion on the border,' and the נידוי lasts until he accepts responsibility for any harm the buyer causes. A new משנה follows: items swapped by customs collectors or bandits, or rescued from a river, soldiers or bandits, belong to the person who has them, because the owners gave up hope (יאוש). The משנה also gives rules about chasing a swarm of bees into someone else's field. The גמרא discusses whether יאוש alone transfers ownership, and how a Jewish or non-Jewish robber affects the owner's hope. It then brings the משנה in כלים about hides held by a גזלן or a גנב. עולא and רבה argue about how far the dispute between the תנא קמא and רבי שמעון reaches, and the גמרא tests their argument against our משנה and a ברייתא about הקדש and תרומה. The amud ends with a second answer: the ברייתא follows רבי, who says a thief is like a robber.

steps.title: The rule applies only to a single witness
steps.stepSummary: The previous rule ends here: a gentile court takes money based on one witness. The גמרא then limits it to a single witness and excludes two witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...based on the word of one witness. And we said this only about one witness, but about two witnesses we did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the sentence from before. It then explains that the נידוי is only for a Jew who testifies alone, not when two witnesses testify together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem with one witness is that a gentile court takes money on his word, while תורה law needs two witnesses for that. When two testify, the outcome matches what a בית דין would do anyway. So nobody lost money unfairly, and there is no reason for נידוי.

keyTerms.meaning: on the word of one witness
we only said this when... (a phrase that limits a rule)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the problem is not testifying in a gentile court as such. The problem is causing a Jew a money loss that a בית דין would not have imposed.

phrases.english: based on the word of one.
phrases.notes: This finishes the line from before: the gentile court takes money from a Jew on just one witness's word.

phrases.english: And we said this only about one,
but about two, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא חַד, אֲבָל בִּתְרֵי לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes and limits the ruling from the previous section about a single witness testifying in a gentile court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נידוי is only for a single witness who testifies against a Jew, not for two witnesses.

steps.title: Even a single witness is only a problem in a village court
steps.stepSummary: A second limit: the single-witness rule applies only in a village court (דיני דמגיסתא). The official government court (בי דוואר) only imposes an oath based on one witness, just as תורה law does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even about one witness, we said this only in a court of villagers. But in the official government court, they too impose only an oath because of one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the rule further. A lone witness is only put in נידוי if he testified in a local village court, not in the official government court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The official court handles one witness the same way תורה law does: one witness leads to an oath, not to taking money. So the Jew being sued loses nothing beyond what a בית דין would require, and the witness did nothing wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: a court of villagers; a local court

steps.whatToRemember: A lone witness against a Jew is put in נידוי only when the court will take money on his word. That means a village court. The official court only imposes an oath, like the תורה does.

phrases.english: And even about one, we did not say this
except in a court of villagers,
but in the official government court,

phrases.aramaic: אִינְהוּ נָמֵי חַד אַמּוֹמְתָא שָׁדוּ לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: they too, because of one witness, only impose an oath on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחַד נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בְּדִינֵי דְמָגִיסְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit on top of the first one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single witness is put in נידוי only in a village court, since the official court only imposes an oath.

steps.title: May an important person whom the gentiles trust like two witnesses testify?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports a question raised in רב הונה's בית מדרש. The gentile courts trust an אדם חשוב as if he were two witnesses. Should he avoid testifying, since they will take money on his word? Or may he testify, since he cannot avoid the authorities?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: When I was in the house of רב הונה, we had a question. An important person whom they rely on like two witnesses: since they take money on his word, should he not testify? Or perhaps, since he is an important person, he cannot avoid them, and he may testify?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings an open question. It applies the rule we just learned to a special case: one person whom the gentiles treat as if he were two witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: because the gentiles take money on his word alone, his testimony works like a single witness in a village court, so he should not testify. Side two: an אדם חשוב cannot hide from the authorities when they demand his testimony, so he is forced into it and is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: a question was raised before us

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוֵינָא בֵּי רַב הוּנָא, אִיבַּעְיָא לַן:
phrases.english: When I was in the house of Rav Huna, a question was asked of us:

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם חָשׁוּב דְּסָמְכִי עֲלֵיהּ כְּבֵי תְרֵי –
phrases.english: an important person whom they rely on like two witnesses,
they take money out on his word,
so he should not testify;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאָדָם חָשׁוּב הוּא –
phrases.english: or perhaps, since he is an important person,
he cannot slip away from them,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the gentile authorities who want his testimony.

phrases.english: and so he may testify?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוֵינָא בֵּי רַב הוּנָא, אִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the single-witness rule to a borderline case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an אדם חשוב, whose single testimony the gentiles accept like two witnesses, may testify against a Jew.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רב אשי's question open with תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the question without an answer. Neither side is proven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source is found to decide between the two sides. So the question about the אדם חשוב remains a תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: let it stand; the question remains unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 3 without resolving it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question about an אדם חשוב testifying in a gentile court remains unresolved.

steps.title: Selling land to a גוי next to a fellow Jew's field brings נידוי
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that a Jew who sells land to a גוי, when that land borders a fellow Jew's field, is put in נידוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: This Jew who sells land to a גוי on the border of his fellow Jew, we put him in נידוי.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב אשי gives another case where a Jew is put in נידוי for causing harm to a fellow Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ruling is stated without a reason. The next steps will figure out why he deserves נידוי.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ אַרְעָא לְגוֹי
phrases.english: This Jew who sells land to a gentile
on the border of his fellow Jew,
we excommunicate him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ אַרְעָא לְגוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case, connected by the shared theme of נידוי for harming a fellow Jew.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew who sells land bordering a fellow Jew's field to a גוי is put in נידוי.

steps.title: What is the reason? Maybe דינא דבר מצרא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason. It suggests the neighbor's right of first purchase, דינא דבר מצרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? If you say it is because of the law of the neighbor on the border...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why he deserves נידוי and offers a first guess. This step sets up the next move, where the guess will be knocked down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דינא דבר מצרא says that when a field is sold, the neighbor whose field borders it gets the first chance to buy. Maybe the seller is punished for skipping that right.

keyTerms.meaning: the bordering neighbor's right of first purchase

phrases.english: What is the reason?

phrases.aramaic: אִי נֵימָא מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא,
phrases.english: If you say it is because of the law of the one on the border,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רב אשי's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why selling such land to a גוי deserves נידוי.

steps.title: דינא דבר מצרא does not apply to sales involving a גוי
steps.stepSummary: The suggested reason is rejected. מר taught that the neighbor's right does not apply when buying from or selling to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't מר say: one who buys from a גוי or sells to a גוי, there is no law of the neighbor on the border!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the first guess. It quotes an established rule that the neighbor's right of first purchase does not apply when a גוי is involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller had no duty to offer the land to his neighbor in the first place, he cannot be punished for failing to. So the נידוי must come from some other reason.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the neighbor has a right of first purchase here. When the buyer is a גוי, דינא דבר מצרא does not apply at all, so the punishment must have a different source.

phrases.english: But didn't the Master say:
one who buys from a gentile, and one who sells to a gentile,
there is no law of the one on the border!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the reason suggested in step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the suggestion that דינא דבר מצרא is the reason for the נידוי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: דינא דבר מצרא does not apply to sales to or from a גוי.

steps.title: The real reason: you placed a lion on my border
steps.stepSummary: The true reason is that the neighbor can say: 'You have put a lion on my border.' The seller brought a possibly dangerous neighbor right next to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because we say to him: You have made a lion lie down on my border.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real reason for the נידוי. The seller harmed his neighbor by bringing in a neighbor who may cause him trouble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is not a lost purchase right. It is the danger and harm the new owner might bring to the Jewish neighbor. The 'lion' is a picture of that threat.

keyTerms.meaning: you made it lie down; you placed

phrases.english: Rather, because we say to him:
phrases.notes: 'We' speak on behalf of the neighbor whose field borders the sold land.

phrases.english: You have made a lion lie down on my border for me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reason with the correct one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seller harmed his neighbor by placing a potentially harmful owner next to him.

steps.title: The נידוי lasts until he accepts responsibility for any harm
steps.stepSummary: Because the problem is possible harm, the נידוי stays in place until the seller accepts responsibility for all damage that comes because of the גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We put him in נידוי until he accepts upon himself any harm that comes because of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes how long the נידוי lasts. It ends once the seller takes responsibility for any harm the new owner causes the neighbor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the reason is the harm to the neighbor, the fix matches that reason. Once the seller guarantees to cover the damage, the neighbor is protected, and the נידוי can be lifted.

keyTerms.meaning: harm or damage that comes by force

steps.whatToRemember: Selling land to a גוי next to a Jew's field brings נידוי. The reason is not דינא דבר מצרא, which does not apply to a גוי. It is that he 'placed a lion on the border.' The נידוי lasts until he accepts responsibility for any resulting harm.

phrases.english: We excommunicate him
until he accepts upon himself
any harm that comes because of him.
phrases.notes: 'Him' here means the גוי buyer; the seller has to cover whatever damage the buyer brings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical result from the reason given in step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The seller stays in נידוי until he takes responsibility for all harm the גוי buyer causes his Jewish neighbor.

steps.title: Customs collectors or bandits swap your item: you may keep it
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that if customs collectors take a person's donkey, or bandits take his garment, and give him a different one in its place, he may keep the replacement, because its owners gave up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If customs collectors took a man's donkey and gave him a different donkey, or bandits took his garment and gave him a different garment, these are now his. This is because the owners have given up hope of getting them back.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that a person may keep a donkey or garment that collectors or bandits gave him in exchange for his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The replacement item was really taken from some other Jew. Still, the משנה lets him keep it, because that other owner has given up hope (יאוש) once robbers took it. Once the owner gives up hope, the item can belong to someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Customs or tax collectors, who often took things by force
Give up hope of getting something back (from the word יֵאוּשׁ)

phrases.english: MISHNA: If customs collectors took his donkey
and gave him a different donkey,
phrases.notes: That other donkey was taken from some other Jew.

phrases.english: or bandits took his garment
and gave him a different garment –
these are his,
because the owners give up hope of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of selling land to a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An item given in exchange by customs collectors or bandits belongs to the receiver, because its owners gave up hope.

steps.title: Rescuing items from a river, soldiers or bandits, and a swarm of bees
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues: someone who rescues items from a river, an army troop or bandits may keep them if the owners gave up hope. The same is true of a swarm of bees.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who rescues things from a river, from a troop of soldiers, or from bandits: if the owners gave up hope, the things are his. And the same is true of a swarm of bees: if the owners gave up hope, they are his.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives more cases where things belong to the finder because the owners gave up hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are cases where the item was almost surely lost to its owner. The key condition is stated outright here: only if the owners actually gave up hope does the rescuer keep it.

keyTerms.meaning: One who rescues or saves something

phrases.english: One who rescues things from the river

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ מִן הַגַּיִיס אוֹ מִן הַלִּסְטִין,
phrases.english: or from a troop of soldiers or from bandits,

phrases.aramaic: אִם נִתְיָיאֲשׁוּ הַבְּעָלִים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: if the owners gave up hope – these are his.
And so too a swarm of bees,
if they gave up hope – these are his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more cases to the same rule about יאוש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rescued items and swarms of bees belong to the one who took them, if the owners gave up hope.

steps.title: Rules about chasing your bees into a friend's field
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה rules that a woman or child is believed about where a swarm came from. The owner may walk into a friend's field to rescue his swarm, paying for any damage, but he may not cut the friend's branch even if he offers to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה said: A woman or a child is believed to say, 'This swarm came out from here.' And a person may walk through his friend's field to rescue his swarm, and if he damages something, he pays for the damage. But he may not cut off his friend's branch, even on condition that he will pay its value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה adds several practical rules about a swarm of bees that flew away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a woman or a child cannot be a witness, but here they are believed about where the bees came from. The owner may enter another's field to save his bees, but he must pay for damage. Cutting the friend's branch goes too far, even with payment.

keyTerms.meaning: The money, the value of the item

steps.confusionAlert: Read 'his branch' (סוכו) as the friend's branch, the tree where the bees landed. It is not the bee owner's branch.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka said:
A woman or a minor is believed
to say: From here this swarm came out.
And he may walk into his friend's field
to rescue his swarm,
and if he caused damage – he pays for what he damaged.
But he may not cut off his branch
on condition that he give the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the swarm of bees case just mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman or child is believed about a swarm's origin. One may enter a friend's field to save his bees and must pay for damage, but may not cut the friend's branch even for payment.

steps.title: The son says: he may cut the branch and pay
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל, the son of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה, disagrees with his father and says the bee owner may even cut the branch and then pay for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל, the son of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה, says: He may even cut the branch and pay its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The son argues with his father on the last point and allows cutting the branch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father forbade cutting the friend's branch even with payment. The son allows it, as long as the owner pays the value afterward.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka, says:
He may even cut it and give the money.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with his father's ruling about cutting the branch.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may cut the friend's branch to save his bees, and must pay its value.

steps.title: A ברייתא: if he took it, he returns it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying that if a person took the swapped item from the collector, he must return it to the original owners. This seems to clash with the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: It was taught in a ברייתא: If he took it, he returns it to the original owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by quoting a ברייתא that seems to go against the משנה's ruling. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the swapped donkey is his. The ברייתא says he must give it back to its first owner. The גמרא now has to explain how the ברייתא sees the case.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught:
If he took it – he returns it to the original owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside source on the first case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who took the swapped item must return it to the original owners.

steps.title: Reading one: giving up hope alone does not transfer ownership
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא holds that יאוש by itself does not make an item belong to someone else. So the item reached him in a forbidden way and must be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: He (the author of the ברייתא) holds that giving up hope alone does not transfer ownership. So from the very start, the item came into his hands in a forbidden way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning of the ברייתא: it disagrees with the משנה about the power of יאוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this ברייתא, the owner giving up hope is not enough to end his ownership. The collector never owned the donkey, so the receiver got a stolen item. That is why he must give it back.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds, he is of the opinion
Giving up hope alone, without any other change
Does not acquire, does not transfer ownership

phrases.english: He holds: giving up hope alone does not acquire,
and from the start it came to his hands in a forbidden way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ברייתא requires returning the item.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the ברייתא follows a different opinion about יאוש.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone agrees with the משנה that the item belongs to him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא holds that יאוש alone does not transfer ownership, so the item must go back.

steps.title: Reading two: if he wants to return it, he returns it
steps.stepSummary: Another version reads the ברייתא differently: it only means that if he chooses to return the item, he should give it to the original owners.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say the ברייתא means: If he comes to return it, he should return it to the original owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to read the ברייתא, which removes the clash with the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, returning the item is not required. The ברייתא is only talking about someone who wants to give it back on his own, and it tells him to give it to the first owners.

keyTerms.meaning: If he comes (chooses) to return it

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
If he comes to return it –
he should return it to the original owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the same ברייתא from step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Returning the item is optional. If he does return it, it goes to the original owners.

steps.title: Why it is optional: giving up hope does transfer ownership
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why returning is not required, and answers that in this version יאוש alone does transfer ownership.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason he does not have to return it? Because giving up hope alone does transfer ownership.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the second reading and answers it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of the first reading. Here, once the owner gave up hope, the item could be acquired, so the receiver truly owns it and has no duty to return it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Giving up hope alone acquires.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the second reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is returning the item only optional?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because יאוש alone transfers ownership, so the item is legally his.

steps.title: If he does not want what is not his, he returns it to the first owner
steps.stepSummary: Even so, if the person says he does not want money that is not truly his, he gives it back to the original owners.
steps.simpleTranslation: However, if he says, 'I do not want money that is not mine,' he returns it to the original owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the second reading: a person who wants to be extra careful gives the item back to its first owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By law the item is his, but a person may choose not to keep property that came from someone else's loss. If he makes that choice, it goes to the original owners.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of the ברייתא. In the first, יאוש alone does not transfer ownership, so the item must be returned. In the second, יאוש alone does transfer ownership, so returning it is only a voluntary act, and if he does it, it goes to the original owners.

phrases.english: However, if he said:
I do not want money that is not mine –
he returns it to the original owners.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיהוּ אִי אָמַר: אִי אֶפְשִׁי בְּמָמוֹן שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the second reading by explaining what 'if he comes to return it' means.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to the second reading, the item legally belongs to the receiver. If he chooses not to keep it, he returns it to the original owners.

steps.title: רב אשי limits the משנה to a non-Jewish bandit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that the swapped items are his because the owners gave up hope. רב אשי says this applies only to a non-Jewish bandit, not a Jewish one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'These are his, because the owners gave up hope.' רב אשי said: they taught this only about a non-Jewish bandit. But with a Jewish bandit, no. The victim thinks: 'Tomorrow I will take him to court.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line in the משנה, and רב אשי adds a limit to it. The rule that the owners gave up hope applies only when a non-Jewish bandit took the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה assumes that when bandits take something, the owners give up hope (יאוש). רב אשי says that is true only for a non-Jewish bandit. If a Jewish bandit stole it, the owner still hopes to drag him to בית דין, so there is no יאוש and the item is not his.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about... (a phrase that limits a rule)
Etc.: the rest of the quoted text is not written out
I will take him to court

phrases.english: These are his,
because the owners, etc.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the משנה. The full line ends: because the owners gave up hope of getting it back.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
They taught this only about a non-Jewish bandit,
but a Jewish bandit, no;
he thinks: tomorrow I will take him to court.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לִסְטִים גּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's line about swapped items to add a new limit to it
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The assumption of יאוש applies only to a non-Jewish bandit. With a Jewish bandit, the victim expects to win in court and does not give up hope.

steps.title: רב יוסף argues the opposite makes more sense
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף objects that a victim of non-Jews does not give up hope, because their courts use force. A victim of a Jew does give up hope, because a Jewish court can only announce a ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף objected: On the contrary, the opposite makes sense! With non-Jews, whose courts judge with force, the victim does not give up hope. With Jews, whose courts only announce a ruling, the victim gives up hope!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף attacks רב אשי's reasoning. He says רב אשי has it backwards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי's whole point was based on how likely the victim is to get the item back through the courts. רב יוסף uses that same reasoning against him. In their situation, the non-Jewish courts could enforce their rulings, but the Jewish courts could not. So it is the victim of a Jewish bandit who would give up hope.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it (a strong challenge)
On the contrary, the opposite makes more sense
They judge with force (they can make people obey)
They only say words (they announce a ruling but cannot force it)
He gives up hope of getting it back

steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף is not saying Jewish courts are less fair. He is saying that, in their time and place, Jewish courts had no power to force anyone to obey. That is why a victim would give up hope.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef objects to it:
On the contrary, the opposite makes sense!
With non-Jews, who judge with force, he does not give up hope;
With Jews, since they only announce a ruling, he gives up hope!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב יוֹסֵף: אַדְּרַבָּה, אִיפְּכָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning of רב אשי's distinction
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that a Jewish bandit's victim does not give up hope
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being able to enforce a ruling is what keeps hope alive. Non-Jewish courts can enforce their rulings, and Jewish courts cannot. So the reverse of רב אשי's distinction is true.

steps.title: Moving רב אשי's statement to the second half of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says that if רב אשי said this, it was about the סיפא. That part of the משנה deals with one who rescues items from non-Jews or bandits, and it lets him keep them only if the owners clearly gave up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if רב אשי said this, he said it about the last part of the משנה: 'One who rescues an item from non-Jews or from bandits, if the owners gave up hope, it is his.' This implies: if the owners gave up hope, yes; if we don't know, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רב יוסף's objection and moves רב אשי's statement to a different line of the משנה. This step sets up the corrected version of רב אשי's statement in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא only lets the rescuer keep the item when we know the owners gave up hope. When we don't know, he may not keep it. This gives a natural place for רב אשי to explain when we can or cannot assume יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, if it was said (introduces a corrected version of a statement)
The later part of a משנה
One who rescues or saves an item
An unclear case, where we don't know what happened

phrases.english: Rather, if it was said,
it was said about the last part:
phrases.notes: This means the later line of the same משנה, not the line about swapped items.

phrases.english: One who rescues from non-Jews and from bandits,
if the owners gave up hope, yes,
if unknown, no.
phrases.notes: If we don't know whether the owners gave up, the rescuer may not keep the item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's objection by moving רב אשי's statement to the סיפא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moving the statement to a different line of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב אשי was talking about the רישא (swapped items), saying a Jewish bandit's victim does not give up hope
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אשי was talking about the סיפא, where יאוש is not assumed in an unclear case

steps.title: The corrected version of רב אשי's statement
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא's rule that we don't assume יאוש in an unclear case applies only to a non-Jewish robber, because his courts use force. With a Jewish bandit, the owner does give up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: They taught this only about a non-Jew, because their courts judge with force. But a Jewish bandit: since the Jewish courts only announce a ruling, the owner gives up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רב אשי's statement in its new form, which now fits רב יוסף's logic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In an unclear case, we cannot assume יאוש when a non-Jew took the item, because the owner can still win back his item through forceful non-Jewish courts. When a Jewish bandit took it, we can assume the owner gave up hope, since the Jewish courts had no power to enforce a ruling. The rule is now the reverse of רב אשי's first version.
steps.whatToRemember: In the final version, a non-Jewish robber means no assumed יאוש, because his courts can enforce their rulings. A Jewish bandit means יאוש is assumed, because the Jewish courts can only announce a ruling. This is the reverse of רב אשי's first version.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. The first version said a Jewish bandit's victim does NOT give up hope. The final version says he DOES.

phrases.english: They taught this only about a non-Jew,
because they judge with force;
but a Jewish bandit,
since they only announce a ruling, he gives up hope.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא גּוֹי, מִשּׁוּם דְּדָיְינִי בְּגֵיתֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the move to the סיפא by giving רב אשי's corrected statement
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the סיפא, the need for clear יאוש applies only to items taken by non-Jews. When a Jewish bandit took the item, יאוש is assumed, because Jewish courts could not enforce their rulings.

steps.title: A משנה about whose thought makes hides able to become impure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה from מסכת כלים. A homeowner's thought makes hides able to become טמא, but a leatherworker's does not. A robber's thought does not, but a thief's does.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: For hides that belong to a homeowner, his thought makes them able to become impure. For hides that belong to a leatherworker, his thought does not. For hides held by a robber, his thought does not make them able to become impure. For hides held by a thief, his thought does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה about leather hides. This sets up a discussion about how יאוש, the owner giving up hope, decides who counts as the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A raw hide can become טמא only once it counts as a finished item. Sometimes just deciding to use it as it is makes it count as finished. The משנה teaches that this decision counts only when it comes from the right person, so the robber and thief cases depend on whether that person counts as the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Thought; a decision about how an item will be used
Makes them able to become טמא
Leatherworker, a craftsman who processes hides
Robber, someone who takes things openly

steps.confusionAlert: "Thought makes them טמא" does not mean the hides become impure right away. It means the thought turns them into a finished item that is now able to become impure.

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in כלים 26:8.

phrases.english: Hides belonging to a homeowner,
thought makes them able to become impure;
phrases.notes: Just deciding to use the hide as it is makes it count as a finished item.

phrases.english: but those of a leatherworker,
thought does not make them able to become impure.
Those of a robber: thought does not make them able to become impure;
and those of a thief: thought makes them able to become impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the discussion of יאוש with bandits and robbers, the גמרא brings a related משנה where יאוש decides whether a robber or thief counts as owner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A homeowner's thought makes hides able to become טמא, but a leatherworker's does not. A robber's thought does not, but a thief's does.

steps.title: רבי שמעון reverses the robber and thief cases
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון says the rule is the other way around. A robber's thought counts and a thief's does not, because the owners have not given up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: The cases are reversed. For hides held by a robber, his thought makes them able to become impure. For hides held by a thief, his thought does not, because the owners have not given up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: Still inside the same משנה, רבי שמעון disagrees with the first opinion. He switches the rulings for the robber and the thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון gives his reason openly: the owners have not given up hope. Without יאוש, the person holding the hide never becomes its owner, so his thought means nothing. Both opinions agree that יאוש is the key. They disagree only about which victim, the one robbed or the one stolen from, gives up hope.

keyTerms.meaning: The matters are reversed; the opposite ruling
Gave up hope (from the word יאוש)
The owners, the people the item was taken from

steps.whatToRemember: In this משנה, a robber's or thief's thought counts only if the real owner gave up hope. The תנא קמא and רבי שמעון disagree about which victim gives up hope.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties the idea of יאוש from our sugya to a completely different area, the laws of טומאה. It shows that יאוש affects who counts as the owner.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
The matters are reversed:
those of a robber, thought makes them able to become impure;
those of a thief, thought does not make them able to become impure;
because the owners have not given up hope.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disagreeing opinion inside the same משנה that reverses the robber and thief rulings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A robber's thought makes hides able to become טמא, but a thief's does not, because the owners of stolen hides have not given up hope.

steps.title: עולא limits the dispute to unclear cases
steps.stepSummary: עולא says the תנא קמא and רבי שמעון argue only when we don't know whether the owners gave up hope. If we know they did, all agree that יאוש acquires.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: The argument is only in a case where we don't know what the owner felt. But where we know the owner gave up hope, everyone agrees that giving up hope makes the item the taker's.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא explains how far the argument from the משנה in כלים (steps 23-24) reaches. He says it only covers cases where we don't know whether the owners gave up hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא and רבי שמעון argued about whether the owner of a stolen item, or of an item taken by force, gives up hope. According to עולא, they were only guessing what an owner usually feels. When the owner clearly gave up hope, nobody argues: יאוש works and the taker owns the hides.

keyTerms.meaning: A dispute or argument between Sages
An unspecified case, where we don't know the facts
A known case, where we know for sure that the owner gave up hope
Giving up hope lets the taker acquire the item

phrases.english: Ulla said:
The dispute is in an unspecified case,
phrases.notes: He means the argument between the תנא קמא and רבי שמעון about the thief and the robber.

phrases.english: but where it is known that the owner gave up hope,
all agree that despair acquires.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets how far the מחלוקת between the תנא קמא and רבי שמעון reaches
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מחלוקת is only in an unclear case. When יאוש is known, everyone agrees it acquires.

steps.title: רבה says they argue even in known cases
steps.stepSummary: רבה disagrees with עולא. He says the מחלוקת exists even when it is known that the owners gave up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Even where it is known that the owner gave up hope, they still argue.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives the opposite view from עולא. He says the argument also covers a case where the owner clearly gave up hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה, the argument is not only a guess about what the owner felt. Even when the owner says he has given up, one side holds that this still does not give the taker ownership, since the owner may still hope to get the item back.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Even where it is known, there is also a dispute.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opposing view to עולא's limit on the מחלוקת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מחלוקת applies even when the owners' יאוש is known.

steps.title: אביי supports עולא from the wording of the mishna
steps.stepSummary: אביי tells רבה not to argue with עולא. The משנה gives רבי שמעון's reason as "because the owners did not give up hope," which implies that if they had, the hides would belong to the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבה: Don't argue with עולא, because the משנה agrees with him. It says: "because the owners did not give up hope." So the reason is only that they did not give up hope. But if they did give up hope, the items would be his!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבה by reading the exact words of the משנה in כלים. He argues that those words prove עולא is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון explains his rule with the words "because the owners did not give up hope." That makes the missing יאוש the only problem. So if the owners clearly did give up hope, even רבי שמעון would agree the thief owns the hides, which is exactly what עולא said.

keyTerms.meaning: Because the owners did not give up hope
The reason is... (an inference from what the reason implies)

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rabba:
Do not disagree with Ulla,
for we learned in the mishna in line with his view:
"Because the owners did not despair."
phrases.notes: This is רבי שמעון's reason from step 24.

phrases.english: The reason is that the owners did not despair,
but if the owners did despair,
these would be his!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַבָּה: לָא תִּיפְלוֹג עֲלֵיהּ דְּעוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבה's view using the wording of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that the מחלוקת exists even when יאוש is known
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון's stated reason is only that the owners did not give up hope. That implies known יאוש would work, which matches עולא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of רבי שמעון in the משנה of כלים

steps.title: רבה reads the mishna with different words
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that he learned the משנה differently: "because owners have no real יאוש." With that wording, there is no proof for עולא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: We learn the משנה as saying, "because there is no giving up hope for the owners."
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers אביי's challenge. He does this by quoting a different wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's proof depended on the words "the owners did not give up hope." רבה's version says owners of stolen goods never truly give up hope, even if they say they have. So even known יאוש would not help according to רבי שמעון, and רבה's view holds.

keyTerms.meaning: There is no (real) giving up hope for the owners

steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not saying that אביי misread the words. He is saying that in his version, the משנה itself has different words.

phrases.english: He said to him:
We, "because there is no despair for the owners,"
phrases.notes: In other words, owners of stolen things never truly give up hope, even if they say they have.

phrases.english: is how we learn it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנַן, לְפִי שֶׁאֵין יֵאוּשׁ לַבְּעָלִים מַתְנִינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה says "the owners did not give up hope," which implies known יאוש would work.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבה's wording says owners have no real יאוש at all, so even known יאוש does not acquire according to רבי שמעון.
steps.whatToRemember: עולא: the argument is only in unclear cases. רבה: they argue even when יאוש is known. Each side reads רבי שמעון's words in the משנה in a way that fits his view.

steps.title: Whose view is the customs-collector mishna?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה about customs collectors who took someone's donkey and asks which תנא it follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: If customs collectors took his donkey, and so on. Whose view is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back our own משנה about customs collectors and asks whose opinion it follows. This sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה lets a person keep the donkey that customs collectors gave him in place of his own, because the owner of that donkey gave up hope. Since the תנא קמא and רבי שמעון argue about when owners give up hope, the גמרא wants to know which of them the משנה matches.

phrases.english: We learned: If customs collectors took his donkey, etc.
Whose view is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה in כלים back to our own משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא, the תנא קמא or רבי שמעון, the customs-collector משנה follows

steps.title: The משנה Fits Neither the רבנן Nor רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says the owner gives up hope both with a customs collector (a גזלן) and with bandits (a גנב). That clashes with the רבנן on one case and with רבי שמעון on the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה follows the רבנן, the robber case is a problem. If it follows רבי שמעון, the thief case is a problem!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the question from the last step. It shows that the משנה does not seem to match either side of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן hold that the owner gives up hope only when a גנב took his item, not when a גזלן took it. רבי שמעון holds the reverse. Our משנה says the owner gives up hope in both cases, so each opinion clashes with one half of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A robber who takes things openly, by force (here, the customs collector)
A thief who takes things secretly (here, the bandits)
It is difficult; this is a problem

phrases.english: If it follows the Rabbis, the robber is difficult,
phrases.notes: The 'robber' is the customs collector in the משנה, who takes the donkey openly.

phrases.english: if it follows Rabbi Shimon, the thief is difficult!
phrases.notes: The 'thief' is the bandits in the משנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי רַבָּנַן – קַשְׁיָא גַּזְלָן, אִי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן – קַשְׁיָא גַּנָּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the question of step 29 by showing that neither תנא fits.
steps.kashyaTarget: Matching the משנה to the רבנן or to רבי שמעון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says the owner gives up hope with both a גזלן and a גנב, but each תנא allows this with only one of them.

steps.title: According to עולא There Is No Problem
steps.stepSummary: עולא holds that when we know the owners gave up hope, everyone agrees the item can be acquired. So the משנה can be a case where this is known, and it fits everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for עולא, who says that when it is known, the person acquires. Here too it is known, and everyone agrees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that עולא's approach solves the problem easily. This sets up the harder question for רבה in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument between the רבנן and רבי שמעון is only about cases where we don't know whether the owner gave up hope. In our משנה the owner clearly gave up hope, so both תנאים agree. The clash from step 30 disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted; this works well (opens a 'works for X, but not for Y' structure)
When it is known (that the owners gave up hope)

phrases.english: Granted, according to Ulla, who said:
when it is known, he acquires;
phrases.notes: This is עולא's view from step 25: when we know the owners gave up hope, everyone agrees יאוש works.

phrases.english: here too it is known, and it is everyone's opinion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30's problem according to עולא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case as one where the יאוש is known, so there is no argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה must follow one side of the argument and clash with the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: For עולא the משנה is a known-יאוש case, where everyone agrees.

steps.title: According to רבה the משנה Fits No One
steps.stepSummary: רבה says the argument exists even when the יאוש is known. So for him the משנה seems to match neither the רבנן nor רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for רבה, who says there is a מחלוקת even when it is known, whose opinion is this משנה? It is neither the רבנן nor רבי שמעון!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the problem against רבה, since עולא's escape route doesn't work for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבה holds the argument applies even to known cases, he cannot say everyone agrees. The clash from step 30 comes right back for him.

phrases.english: But according to Rabba, who said:
even when it is known, there is a dispute;
whose opinion is this?
Not the Rabbis and not Rabbi Shimon!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְרַבָּה, דְּאָמַר: בְּיָדוּעַ נָמֵי מַחְלוֹקֶת; הָא מַנִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second half of the 'בשלמא... אלא' structure: it works for עולא but not for רבה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's view that the argument applies even when the יאוש is known
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the 'everyone agrees in a known case' answer, the משנה clashes with each תנא.

steps.title: The Bandits Are Armed, So the משנה Follows רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The bandits in the משנה are armed. That makes them like robbers, so both cases in the משנה are robbers, and the משנה follows רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is armed bandits, and the משנה follows רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבה by redefining the bandits in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Armed bandits take things openly by force, the same way a גזלן does. So the 'thief' problem for רבי שמעון disappears. רבי שמעון holds that the victim of a robber gives up hope, and that fits both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Armed bandits, who rob openly with weapons

phrases.english: It is about an armed bandit,
and it follows Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 32's challenge against רבה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the bandits are armed, so they count as robbers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bandits were treated as a גנב, which clashes with רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bandits are armed robbers, so the whole משנה follows רבי שמעון.

steps.title: Then the Bandit Case Repeats the Robber Case
steps.stepSummary: If the armed bandit is a robber, he is the same as the customs collector, so why does the משנה teach both?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, this is the same as the robber!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave: it seems to make the משנה repeat itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The customs collector case already teaches that a robber's victim gives up hope. If the armed bandit is also a robber, the second case seems to add nothing.

phrases.english: If so, this is the same as the robber!
phrases.notes: The 'robber' here is the customs collector from the first case in the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the bandits are armed robbers
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both cases are robbers, the משנה is repeating itself for no reason.

steps.title: The משנה Teaches Two Kinds of Robbers
steps.stepSummary: The משנה deliberately teaches two different types of robbers: the customs collector and the armed bandit.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are two types of robbers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the repetition is on purpose, because each case shows a different kind of robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The customs collector and the armed bandit both take things openly, but they are different types of robbers. The משנה lists both to show that the rule holds for each. This settles רבה's reading of the משנה.
steps.whatToRemember: For עולא, the משנה is a known-יאוש case that everyone agrees to. For רבה, it follows רבי שמעון: the bandits are armed robbers, and the משנה teaches two kinds of robbers.

phrases.english: Two types of robber.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the repetition challenge of step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the repetition: the two cases are two different types
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both cases are the same kind of robber, so one is extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה teaches two distinct types of robbers: the customs collector and the armed bandit.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: what thieves and robbers set aside counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: when a גנב, a גזלן or an אנס makes something הקדש, or separates תרומה or מעשר, it takes effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A thief, a robber, and one who forces a sale: what they make holy is holy, their תרומה is תרומה, and their מעשר is מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to test the argument between עולא and רבה. This step only quotes the ברייתא; the questions come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only make something הקדש or תרומה if it is yours. So the ברייתא assumes that in all three cases the owner gave up hope and the taker now owns the item.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who forces the owner to sell to him
Something made holy for the בית המקדש

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A thief, a robber, and one who forces a sale:
what they consecrate is consecrated,
and their teruma is teruma, and their tithes are tithes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new test of the עולא and רבה argument, after the earlier משנה was settled in Step 35.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a known יאוש lets anyone acquire the item (עולא) or whether the dispute still applies (רבה)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about the הקדש, תרומה and מעשר of a גנב, גזלן and אנס

steps.title: The ברייתא fits neither side
steps.stepSummary: Whose view is this? The רבנן would have trouble with the robber, and רבי שמעון would have trouble with the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is it? If it is the רבנן, the robber is a problem. If it is רבי שמעון, the thief is a problem!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which תנא the ברייתא follows, and shows it seems to fit nobody.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן hold that a robber's victim does not give up hope, so the robber does not own the item. רבי שמעון holds that a thief's victim does not give up hope. The ברייתא says all three acquire, so each side has one case that does not fit.

phrases.english: Whose view is it?
If it is the Rabbis, the robber is difficult,
phrases.notes: For the רבנן, a robber does not own what he took, yet here his הקדש works.

phrases.english: if it is Rabbi Shimon, the thief is difficult!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא quoted in Step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a thief and a robber both acquire
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each תנא holds that one of these two does not acquire, so the ברייתא matches neither.

steps.title: For עולא, the case is a known יאוש
steps.stepSummary: עולא holds that when the יאוש is known, everyone agrees the taker acquires. So the ברייתא is that kind of case and fits everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for עולא, who says that when the יאוש is known, he acquires. Here too it is known, and it is everyone's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the problem goes away easily according to עולא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן and רבי שמעון only argue when we are not sure whether the owner gave up hope. If the ברייתא is talking about a case where we know he did, all three takers acquire according to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: Where it is known that the owner gave up hope

phrases.english: It works well for Ulla,
who says that where it is known, he acquires;
here too it is a case where it is known,
and it is the view of everyone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 37 according to עולא, the same way as Step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case as one where the יאוש is known
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא has to follow one side of the dispute.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a case of known יאוש there is no dispute, so it fits everyone.

steps.title: For רבה, the problem remains
steps.stepSummary: רבה holds the argument applies even when the יאוש is known, so for him the ברייתא still fits neither the רבנן nor רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for רבה, who says the argument applies even when the יאוש is known, whose view is this? Neither the רבנן nor רבי שמעון!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the 'known יאוש' answer is not open to רבה, so the question comes back against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since for רבה the dispute holds even in a known case, he cannot use עולא's way out. The ברייתא now looks like a challenge to רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: But (moving to the side that has the problem)

phrases.english: But according to Rabba,
who says that even where it is known there is a dispute;
whose view is this?
Neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Shimon!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְרַבָּה, דְּאָמַר בְּיָדוּעַ נָמֵי מַחְלוֹקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the problem from Step 37 against רבה, matching Step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's view that the dispute applies even when the יאוש is known
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the 'known יאוש' way out, the ברייתא contradicts both תנאים.

steps.title: The thief here is an armed bandit
steps.stepSummary: The 'thief' in the ברייתא is an armed bandit, who counts as a robber. So the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is talking about an armed bandit, and it follows רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבה with the same move it used for the earlier משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An armed bandit takes by force, so he is treated like a robber, not a secret thief. For רבי שמעון a robber's victim gives up hope, so the 'thief' acquires too.

phrases.english: Here too, it is talking about an armed bandit,
phrases.notes: 'Here too' points back to the same answer given for the משנה in Step 33.

phrases.english: and it is the view of Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 39 for רבה, the same way as Step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the 'thief' as an armed bandit
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גנב in the ברייתא is an ordinary secret thief, which רבי שמעון cannot accept.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is an armed bandit, really a kind of robber, so the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון.

steps.title: Then he is just a robber
steps.stepSummary: If the 'thief' is really a robber, he is the same as the גזלן already listed, so why mention both?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, he is the same as the robber!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: the answer seems to make the ברייתא repeat itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already lists a גזלן. If the גנב is also a robber, there is no reason to list him separately.

phrases.english: If so, this is the same as a robber!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 40, like Step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the גנב in the ברייתא as an armed bandit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It makes the ברייתא list the same kind of person twice.

steps.title: Two kinds of robbers
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is teaching two different types of robbers: the ordinary robber and the armed bandit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two types of robbers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא lists both on purpose, and this settles the ברייתא for רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both are robbers in law, but they are different types, so the ברייתא names each one. With that, the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון and is no proof against רבה.
steps.whatToRemember: This ברייתא is no proof for עולא. רבה can explain it just like the earlier משנה: the 'thief' is an armed bandit, a second kind of robber, and the ברייתא follows רבי שמעון.

phrases.english: Two types of robbers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 41 and closes this proof, like Step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining why the list is not repetitive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing the armed bandit and the robber separately is pointless repetition.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are two different types of robbers, so both are named.

steps.title: Another answer: the ברייתא follows רבי, who says a thief is like a robber
steps.stepSummary: Instead of reading 'thief' as an armed bandit, the גמרא says the ברייתא means a real thief. It follows רבי, who holds in another ברייתא that a thief is treated like a robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: this ברייתא follows רבי. As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי says: a thief is like a robber.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer to the earlier problem with the ברייתא. It brings a source showing that רבי gives a thief the same law as a robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer had to change the meaning of 'thief' into an armed bandit, so it could fit רבי שמעון's rule about robbers. This answer keeps 'thief' meaning a plain thief. Because רבי gives a thief the same law as a robber, the ברייתא can treat them the same way without any reinterpretation.

keyTerms.meaning: "And if you want, say...": introduces a second, alternative answer
Here it means a ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה
A thief, someone who steals secretly
A robber, someone who takes openly by force

steps.confusionAlert: This does not reject the armed-bandit answer. It is simply another way to answer the same question. Both answers stay on the table.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
this ברייתא follows the view of רבי;
as it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי says:
a thief is like a robber,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא מַתְנִיתָא – רַבִּי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, alternative answer to the problem in step 39, alongside the armed-bandit answer of steps 40 to 42.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ברייתא to a different תנא (רבי) whose rule makes it fit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'thief' had to be explained as an armed bandit to fit רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'thief' can be a real thief, because the ברייתא follows רבי, who gives a thief the same law as a robber.
steps.raayaObject: That some תנא gives a thief the same law as a robber.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: רבי אמר גנב כגזלן.
